title: Long-tail network & KV fallback dissection - Zephyr Therapeutics
summary: Deep dive on p95/p99 tail causes for Zephyr's inference endpoint. Focus on network hop amplification, KV-cache hot-shard behavior, streaming vs non-streaming latencies, and fallbacks for on-prem/VPC topologies. Agreed next steps: run targeted microbenchmarks, share topology diagram, provide security checklist, and propose pilot config with an autoscale + cache warming plan.
action_items: Maya Chen - send microbenchmark template and sample results by 2027-10-13
Daniel Ortiz - capture model/system perf knobs and recommended quantization profiles by 2027-10-15
Marcus Lee - share VPC topology diagram and current subnet routing rules by 2027-10-12
Sofia Alvarez - request SOC2 appendix and KMS integration docs from Redwood by 2027-10-14
next_steps: Run targeted p99 microbench with 1000 concurrent single-token streaming requests (Zephyr to run and share logs)
Redwood to propose Pilot config: 2x dedicated nodes, prefix caching enabled, conservative batch size, quantized FP16+int8 profile
Schedule follow-up check-in to review benchmark results week of 2027-10-18
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Zephyr Head of ML), Marcus Lee (Platform Eng), Sofia Alvarez (SecOps), Tom Hsu (SRE), Alyx Reed (ML Eng)

[00:00:05] Maya (Redwood - AE): all right everyone, thank you for carving out time. we wanted to focus today's session on the long tail you're seeing at zephyr for your primary chat-inference endpoint. specifically p95/p99 blowups that happen intermittently. we brought daniel to dig into runtime and topology. feel free to interrupt.

[00:00:22] Priya (Zephyr): thanks maya. yes we've got production alerts about p99 spikes that are killing SLAs for a subset of requests. usually during deployments or network churn, but sometimes it just flares for no apparent reason.

[00:00:35] Daniel (Redwood - SE): cool. quick sanity check: are most requests short-context, single-turn assistant messages or is there a lot of long-history chat?

[00:00:42] Alyx (Zephyr): primary load is single-turn 40-100 token prompts, about 25 rps sustained per endpoint, bursts to 200 rps during peak. we also have 5% multi-turn flows that hit 2k tokens.

[00:00:55] Daniel: perfect, that's helpful. two immediate hypotheses for tail: network hop amplification (inter-subnet routing or NAT timeouts), and KV cache hot-shard/eviction events causing cold-LR cache reads. plus, streaming vs non-streaming call mode can change how the runtime schedules and prioritizes requests.

[00:01:15] Tom (SRE): we've already instrumented infra metrics; we saw occasional 10-20x increase in service-to-backend RTTs when p99 spikes occur but not CPU/GPU saturation. so network looks suspicious.

[00:01:30] Marcus (Platform): to add, our VPC layout is multi-subnet with cross-az peering; some legacy NAT gateways still exist for outbound. could those be the hop?

[00:01:41] Daniel: absolutely. NATs and cross-az proxies can add jitter. also, some serialization layers we use (gRPC vs http/2, muxed connections) may react poorly to lost keep-alives. one more: KV cache hot-shards — if a single shard gets hammered, latency for misses cascades. we've seen scenarios where a transient hotkey causes a synchronous backend fetch that blocks the request thread.

[00:02:05] Priya: that's what we suspect. We instrumented cache miss rate spikes aligning with p99 events. how do you typically recommend diagnosing whether it's network vs cache?

[00:02:16] Daniel: do a bisection: run microbenchmarks that isolate the layers. two parallel tests: 1) On-node synthetic requests hitting local cache (bypass network) to see if runtime latency holds; 2) End-to-end tests from your client subnets that reproduce the production route. compare forked traces. if local is tight but end-to-end shows spike, it's network or inter-service routing. if both spike, it's runtime or model-level issue — e.g., cache eviction or kv fetch stall.

[00:02:45] Maya: we can provide a microbenchmark harness. it will run streaming and non-streaming patterns, single-token vs 100-token, and capture per-hop timing. we'll share it with marcus.

[00:02:58] Marcus: please do. also can you remind us the difference in scheduling behavior for streaming vs non-streaming in your runtime? we've seen cases where switching modes reduced tails, but not always.

[00:03:12] Daniel: yes. short version: streaming requests are scheduled to start emitting partial tokens as soon as possible, the runtime can interleave many streaming requests more aggressively which reduces queuing for short tokens — but it also increases the number of context switches and can amplify noise if a single request stalls mid-stream. non-streaming (batching) prefers to aggregate tokens up to a batch threshold, which can reduce per-token cost and variance at the expense of slightly higher median latency. so streaming often helps median for short responses but can worsen p99 if you have network instability or if there's a long-tail stall in the middle of the stream.

[00:03:52] Priya: interesting, so for us with mostly short single-turn messages, streaming should help medians but maybe worsens p99 when network is flaky. is there a hybrid?

[00:04:01] Daniel: yes — hybrid heuristics: start in non-streaming mode with a micro-batch size of 2-4 for a short window, then fall back to streaming if the response length exceeds threshold. Redwood's SDK supports a fallthrough policy. that reduces context-switch overhead for tiny replies while still streaming larger outputs.

[00:04:18] Alyx: we do see the worst p99s coincide with post-deploys. could cold cache + inter-az routing create a compound effect?

[00:04:26] Daniel: totally. example sequence: deploy causes reuse of a different node, prefix cache isn't warmed, first few requests hit a remote key-value store (or on-disk store in private deployment) which is on a different AZ, network RTT spikes, and the runtime gets blocked waiting for KV fetch. That single long request can dominate tail percentiles because queues back up behind it.

[00:04:48] Tom: on our side we have metrics showing increased disk I/O on our on-prem redis instances during those windows. sometimes eviction spikes as well.

[00:04:56] Daniel: eviction thrash is a classic. if the cache uses LRU and your access distribution shifts post-deploy (new model variants, new prefix tokens), hot keys can move and cause cache churn. two mitigations: warm the prefix cache proactively during rollout, and implement request-rate-limiting or circuit breakers for heavy-key flows so they don't cascade.

[00:05:15] Priya: warm the prefix cache — is that an automated Redwood feature or do we need to run a job?

[00:05:22] Maya: we have a cache-warming utility in our pilot scripts. it can pre-populate KV for pinned prefixes. for Dedicated/Private deployments we can include a warm-up step as part of the rolling deploy. we'll send the script.

[00:05:31] Marcus: regarding quantization — we're using FP16 for inference. could quantization cause variance? we've been experimenting with int8 but worried about perf anomalies.

[00:05:40] Daniel: quantization itself typically changes throughput and per-token compute variance a little; int8 kernels often have different micro-batching benefits. the main risk for tails is mixed-precision fallback behavior: if the runtime encounters a kernel it can't run on the chosen quantization path it may fallback to a slower kernel or CPU path, and that fallback can create outliers. so we recommend validating the quantized kernels offline and turning on kernel-compatibility checks in the runtime to avoid silent fallbacks.

[00:06:05] Alyx: that makes sense. On our on-prem cluster, some nodes have slightly older GPUs; could heterogenous hardware cause silent fallbacks?

[00:06:12] Daniel: yes — heterogeneity is a big source of tail jitter. runtime tries to schedule to compatible devices but if capacity forces placement onto older hardware, you can see p99 spikes. two strategies: label pools by capability and route requests by profile, or use node-compatibility routing that prefers modern kernels and only spills over under load with explicit fallbacks.

[00:06:30] Priya: what about cross-region? we have a backup region for DR, and sometimes routing temporarily sends traffic there. can that explain sudden large p99s?

[00:06:38] Daniel: absolutely — cross-region RTT is huge compared to intra-az. If your routing policy isn't strict about region affinity for real-time endpoints, that can create big outliers. implement region affinity with a small grace period for retries; if a region is unhealthy, fail fast to a local variant rather than cross-region synchronous call.

[00:06:55] Marcus: we have RBAC and SSO rules that route a small % of traffic through an inspection proxy. could that proxy be the cause?

[00:07:01] Sofia (SecOps): yes, we route certain flagged requests for inspection. it's low-volume but maybe it correlates with p99 spikes. we can lift that policy during load tests.

[00:07:08] Daniel: great. for diagnosis we recommend toggling any inspection proxies and running bench tests to compare. also capture end-to-end traces with per-hop timing — even span-level micro timestamps.

[00:07:20] Maya: we'll provide a tracing SDK snippet that annotates the KV fetch, the model exec, and the network hops. that helps isolate whether the stall is inside the runtime or on network calls.

[00:07:29] [00:07:29] Priya: ok. one thing: our users care about deterministic p99s for SLAs. what are pragmatic safeguards if we can't get p99 down to target?

[00:07:38] Daniel: two classes of safeguards: graceful degradation and redundancy. graceful degradation: fall back to a smaller but faster model variant or return a cached paraphrase when latency crosses a threshold. redundancy: maintain a warm standby pool in the same AZ that you failover to with a fast health check, and use request hedging for critical reads (issue two parallel requests to different pools and take the first). hedging increases cost but reduces p99 significantly.

[00:08:02] Marcus: hedging might be ok for a subset of premium traffic. can Redwood's console help audit hedging cost vs p99 benefit?

[00:08:09] Maya: yes the Console shows token-level cost, hedging overhead, and per-route p99 impact. we can demo cost tradeoffs in the pilot.

[00:08:16] Alyx: question on monitoring: what metrics should we add to detect hot-key induced tail events early?

[00:08:24] Daniel: besides per-request latency histograms, export per-key access frequency and per-shard latencies for KV backend. alert on deviation from typical access entropy (if entropy drops and a few keys take >X% of reads) and on increase in variance of fetch times per shard. also instrument kernel fallback counts and per-kernel exec time for quantized vs non-quantized paths.

[00:08:47] Tom: good, we can push those metrics into our telemetry pipeline.

[00:08:52] Priya: we'd like a concrete experiment plan. can we outline steps?

[00:08:58] Maya: yes. high-level plan: (1) Marcus shares topology and routing rules; (2) Redwood provides microbench harness and tracing snippet; (3) Zephyr runs two bench sets: local-only (bypass network) and end-to-end; (4) compare traces and identify layer at fault; (5) run deployment with cache warm and hedging enabled on a small subset; (6) measure p99 delta.

[00:09:21] Alyx: timeline? we can run item 3 this week if you send the harness now.

[00:09:26] Maya: we'll send today. action: maya to send microbench and warm-up scripts.

[00:09:32] [00:09:32] Priya: thank you. also security — sofia will want encryption-at-rest and KMS integration verified for the KV store used by Redwood in Private mode.

[00:09:42] Sofia: yes please send SOC2 and KMS docs. we need to see key rotation policies and audit log examples.

[00:09:49] Maya: noted, will include SOC2 appendix and KMS integration guide.

[00:09:53] Daniel: couple more technical notes I wanted to call out: (a) if your KV backend is on the same subnet but exposed via a managed redis that sits behind a proxy, the proxy can create sync stalls under connection saturation — suggest increasing connection pools and using pooled async clients; (b) consider prefix-anchored caching for chat histories to reduce key cardinality; (c) for quantization, pin node pools by kernel compatibility.

[00:10:18] Marcus: can you elaborate on prefix-anchored caching?

[00:10:21] Daniel: sure — instead of caching per full prompt, cache common prefix embeddings/kv entries that many users share (e.g., system prompt, standard context). that reduces unique key cardinality and makes hot keys more predictable and easier to warm.

[00:10:36] Priya: interesting. may add some upfront memory cost but should reduce misses.

[00:10:40] Maya: one more operational thing: when rolling out new model variants, do a canary traffic split with a small percentage pinned to warm nodes, run warm-up, then increase traffic. that's in our rollout recipe.

[00:10:52] Tom: on the SRE side we'll temporarily disable extra inspection proxies and NAT for the bench window to reduce variables.

[00:10:58] Daniel: great. also if you can capture a flamegraph from the runtime during a spike, that helps. we'll provide the debug flags.

[00:11:07] Alyx: will do.

[00:11:10] Priya: quick question — if we go with Dedicated vs Private, are there differences in how caching behaves?

[00:11:16] Daniel: yes slightly. Dedicated (hosted but reserved) uses Redwood-managed KV caches colocated with runtime nodes and benefits from our optimized in-memory tier; Private on-prem will surface your existing KV infra which may be disk-backed or use customer-managed redis. so Private requires more careful cache sizing and warm-up planning. also private deployments may have network constraints that change scheduling heuristics.

[00:11:37] Sofia: that matches what we feared. we'll probably do a Dedicated pilot first to prove out the SLOs, then replicate on-prem.

[00:11:44] Maya: sounds like a reasonable path.

[00:11:47] [00:11:47] Priya: ok, wrapping up — quick recap and owners?

[00:11:52] Maya: recap: (1) Redwood sends microbench harness, warm-up scripts, tracing SDK snippet, SOC2/KMS docs (Owner: Maya) ; (2) Zephyr shares VPC topology and routing rules + run benches (Owner: Marcus & Priya) ; (3) Redwood provides quantization/kernel compatibility checklist and debug flags (Owner: Daniel) ; (4) Follow-up check-in week of 2027-10-18 to review results.

[00:12:16] Priya: thanks. one last oddity — sometimes a small % of requests have repeated token echoing, maybe a model issue. is that likely related?

[00:12:24] Daniel: usually token echoing is model/config drift or truncation errors, not network. but if a partial stream got dropped and retried, you might see duplication. include sample logs and we'll triage.

[00:12:33] Alyx: we'll attach examples with bench runs.

[00:12:36] Maya: perfect. action items spelled out in the notes. any final q's?

[00:12:42] Sofia: none from security — just the docs.

[00:12:45] Marcus: no. thanks team.

[00:12:48] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[00:12:52] [00:12:52] -- end main discussion -- remainder of call used for quick technical clarifications --

[00:13:10] Daniel: small note on the hedging implementation — if you hedge make sure the backend de-duplicates logs so billing and observability remain sane.

[00:13:20] Marcus: good point.

[00:13:23] Daniel: also watch out for increased KV backend load; hedging can multiply reads unless you short-circuit cache on duplicates.

[00:13:31] Priya: ok noted.

[00:13:36] Maya: I'll list all the artifacts in the follow-up email including links: microbench harness (link: https://redwood.ai/pilot/microbench), warmup scripts (link: https://redwood.ai/pilot/warmup), SOC2 appendix (link: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2), KMS guide (link: https://redwood.ai/security/kms-integration).

[00:13:55] Tom: thanks. we'll run the benches in an isolated window and share the raw traces.

[00:14:01] Priya: thank you, team. talk soon.

[00:14:05] Maya: thanks everyone, bye.

[00:14:09] [00:14:09] call ended

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: 'KV' transcribed sometimes as 'K V' or 'K V cash', 'hedging' occasionally transcribed as 'heading'. speaker labels may blur near the end; timestamps are approximate every 15-60 seconds.
